metas.name: Albania - horizontal bars
metas.note:
Other, more simple Albanian pole tops will often have horizontal bars.

NOTE: If you are not sure between Montenegro or Albania and see these poles, guess Albania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Albania - triangle top
metas.note:
These pole tops, with an upside down triangle shape, are a good clue for Albania.

NOTE: Serbia, Czechia, Slovakia and Romania use similar pole tops.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/albania.

metas.name: Argentina - B Type - cap
metas.note: B Type with a cap on top featuring a lower bar with 2 insulator racks facing downwards and a one-sided bar above it with more down-facing insulators.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/argentina.

metas.name: Argentina - B Type - insulators facing Up
metas.note: B-Type with insulators facing up featuring a lower bar with 2 insulator racks facing upwards and a one-sided bar above it with more up-facing insulators.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - B Type - no top
metas.note: This is a variant of the B type pole where the vertical bar ends at the top horizontal bar unlike the standard version where it extends past it.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - B Type - short top
metas.note: B-Type short top - In this variant, the vertical bar only extends a very small amount past the top horizontal bar, less than the length between the two horizontal bars.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - B Type - standard length top
metas.note: In this variant, the vertical beam extends above the top horizontal bar at roughly about the same length between the two horizontal bars.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - B Type - wooden
metas.note: A wooden variant of the B Type pole.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - C Type - no cap
metas.note: C Type Pole, where there are 3 alternating horizontal beams with down-facing insulators on the end of each of them. In this variant there is no cap on top.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - C Type - short cap
metas.note: Short cap is where the vertical beam extends above the top horizontal bar a distance less than the distance less than the distance between the other horizontal beams.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - D Type
metas.note: It has no other horizontal beams except the one on top which has a unique shape to the other types of poles in Argentina. It can be found everywhere but there are region where there less common.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - silver plate
metas.note: White vertical pole stickers with several digits can be found in Tucumán.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Argentina - single insulator
metas.note: In Mendoza, poles with a single insulator attached to the side of the pole can be found.
metas.footer: Source: Complete Guide to Argentina Poletops by Kyleb.b

metas.name: Argentina - wooden hook poles
metas.note: Within Argentina, these Latvian style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/argentina for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - angled upwards
metas.note: Queensland features these unique pole tops with coils that are angled upwards on the sides.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - black markings
metas.note: These black markings are specific to electricity poles in Queensland. They are often accompanied by diagonal numbers.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - blue circular sticker
metas.note:
Circular blue stickers can be found on Queensland poles. You may occasionally see the same type of sticker in a different colour, or with the colour almost completely faded.

NOTE: Blue stickers can also be found on French poles.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - blue square
metas.note: Melbourne poles commonly feature these white, rectangular stickers, with a smaller blue square inside it.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - concret pole
metas.note: According to a 2006 review, 64% of all concrete poles are located in the state of Victoria.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - marking bands
metas.note: Poles in Western Australia often have green painted bases, and sometimes a white sticker or a red and white band attached.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - rusty metal pole
metas.note:
These rusty metal poles, containing several holes, are unique to the Northern Territory.

NOTE: These poles can also sometimes be found in some areas of northern WA, such as Wyndham.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - stobie pole
metas.note:
The iconic Stobie pole, made of steel and concrete, is specific to South Australia. The pole tops (trident or rotated letter “E”) are also unique.

NOTE: A few thousand of these poles can be found in other states, most notably Tasmania.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - tas pole
metas.note:
Poletops in Tasmania often consist of a thin metal crossbar bent 90 degrees to form an L-shape.

NOTE: Regular Australian crossbars are usually made out of wood.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - trident pole
metas.note: A trident-like pole top can sometimes be seen in Western Australia and Victoria.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Australia - victoria pole
metas.note: Victorian pole tops feature 3 circular coils; 2 on the sides, and 1 vertical one at the top. At times, other extensions can be seen on these poles.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/australia for more clues.

metas.name: Belgium - poles
metas.note:
Most poles in Belgium are concrete, square shaped, and have tiny holes running up them. They often have small metal wrappings around them. The second most common type of pole has oval-shaped holes. You can find many different types of concrete poles in Belgium.

NOTE: The small metal wrappings can be found in France as well.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Bolivia - Curvy poles
metas.note:
Many wooden utility poles, particularly in the eastern parts of Bolivia’s Street View coverage, are noticeably curvy and look like they are made from locally sourced tree trunks.

NOTE: While you may see slightly bent poles in other places, extremely curvy poles are a very good clue for Bolivia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bolivia.

metas.name: Botswana - pole
metas.note:
In Botswana, most poles are generic wooden poles with a wooden top.

NOTE: South Africa also use this type of pole
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/botswana for more clues.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - 1-top 2-alternating insulators
metas.note: Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/brazil for more clues.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - black double UFO-shaped
metas.note: Poles with these black double UFO-shaped insulators in a trident formation are common in Maranhão. The insulator itself is common across many states, but not in this configuration.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - brown mushroom
metas.note: Insulators that resemble brown mushrooms are only found in Pernambuco.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - dark brown insulators
metas.note: These dark brown insulators with grey bases are found almost exclusively in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/brazil for more clues.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - grey Lollipop
metas.note: These insulators are spherical or cone shaped and suspended on a rod above the insulator bar. They are often referred to as “lollipop” insulators. They are very common in Rio Grande de Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and more rarely, Sergipe.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - horizontal
metas.note: Poles with horizontal insulators are very common in Pará and less so in Mato Grosso. They are rarely found in Acre, Amapá, Tocantins, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - long grey
metas.note:
Long grey insulators, not including when they are horizontal, are most commonly found in Pará, Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Bahia, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná and Santa Catarina.

They are found rarely in Maranhão, Rio Grande do Norte, Alagoas, Sergipe, Rondônia, and Rio Grande do Sul. Other states have between 0 and 5%.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - long thin
metas.note: Insulators in Ceará can sometimes be uniquely long and thin. They are in Goiás too, but are rare.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - spool of thread
metas.note: These insulators have a shape resembling a spool of thread. They are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - transparent
metas.note: Transparent insulators are mostly in Alagoas in the northeast, and Santa Catarina in the south. They can be seen rarely in Sergipe, Ceará, and Brasília.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Insulators - white mushrooms
metas.note: Insulators that resemble white mushrooms are found in Bahia and rarely Brasília.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Marker - black paint
metas.note: Pole IDs in Paraná are usually made up of black paint and yellow or white painted text.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Marker - long yellow paint with letter
metas.note: Markings on poles are used by the electricity companies to identify them. This pole ID is long, yellow pole paint with a black code. The ones that start with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/brazil for more clues.

metas.name: Brazil - Marker - long yellow/black paint
metas.note: Similar to the Bahia and Pernambuco poles, Goiás poles also use long, yellow pole paint with a black paint code, but it always starts with a number. They also have a rarer yellow on black pole ID, which can be either paint or a plate.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Marker - paint with street name
metas.note: Utility poles in Paraná on intersections are sometimes painted with the street name. This can sometimes extend to Santa Catarina or Rio Grande do Sul if there are ladder poles in the city.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Marker - small beige plate with numbers
metas.note: Most poles in Maranhão have a small beige plate with numbers built into the surface of the pole. This pole ID can be found in Pará and Piauí more rarely.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Marker - small yellow/orange plate
metas.note: This small yellow or orange plate attached onto the pole by thin metal or zip tie is found in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco. This ID is usually much higher up the pole in Pernambuco than in Rio Grande do Norte.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Marker - square yellow
metas.note: São Paulo has a square, yellow pole ID paint. It has three letters on top followed by two numbers, a black line, and four more numbers. The three letters represent the municipality within São Paulo, but are rarely visible.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Pole - round poles
metas.note:
Alongside ladder poles, round poles can often be found across the south of Brazil, especially São Paulo. These poles are cylindrical and made of concrete.

NOTE: This map and the following wooden pole map was created using statistical analysis of semi-urban and rural locations. 434 locations of 3 poles per location were used across 16 states that were thought to have mixed poles. Regardless of the state, the centre of large cities will often have round poles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Pole - wooden poles
metas.note: Some states also use wooden poles. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Poletop - asymmetrical crossbar with no support
metas.note:
This asymmetrical crossbar with no supports is exclusive to Ceara and Rondonia.

NOTE: While the crossbar in Ceara is usually made of concrete, the Rondonian variation features a metal crossbar, and is far less common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Poletop - asymmetrical crossbar with support
metas.note: This poletop, consisting of an asymmetrical crossbar and a support reaching to the middle of the longer part of the crossbar, is the most common poletop in the state of São Paulo. It can also be frequently seen in the states of Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro and Mato Grosso do Sul.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Poletop - electircity boxes on top
metas.note:
Gamma-shaped poles containing electricity boxes at the end of the bar are most commonly seen in the state of Rio de Janeiro and in the cities of Belém, Salvador, Fortaleza and Maceió.

NOTE: A variation with a shorter bar is exclusive to Belém.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Poletop - João-de-Barro nests
metas.note: These spheres on top of utility poles are João-de-Barro nests. They are common across the south of Brazil.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Poletop - pencil pole
metas.note: Poles that have a smooth cone on top, often called a pencil pole, are common in the state of Rio de Janeiro and rarely in Brasília and Manaus.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Brazil - Poletop - zig-zag top bar
metas.note: This pole configuration, featuring a zigzag-shaped top bar resting atop a flat crossbar, is exclusive to Ceara and Roraima. The pole is usually much larger than a regular electricity pole.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/brazil.

metas.name: Bulgaria - Alternating pole top
metas.note: Most poles have small, alternating hook-shaped insulators.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Bulgaria - small alternating hooks
metas.note:
This style of pole top, with 3 large, alternating insulators that are shaped like upward facing hooks, is a good clue for Bulgaria. This pole top is probably unique to the country.

NOTE: You can also find this pole top with the insulators facing downwards.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/bulgaria.

metas.name: Cambodia - round pole
metas.note:
Round concrete poles with small holes. These are also pretty common in Vietnam.

NOTE: You can easily distinguish between Thailand and Cambodia based on the poles. Thailand uses square concrete poles with rows of small pinholes on the sides. Such poles are very uncommon in Cambodia (but not completely absent).
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/cambodia.

metas.name: Cambodia - waffel
metas.note:
Concrete ladder poles (so named because the indents and ridges resemble a ladder).

NOTE: You can easily distinguish between Thailand and Cambodia based on the poles. Thailand uses square concrete poles with rows of small pinholes on the sides. Such poles are very uncommon in Cambodia (but not completely absent).
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/cambodia.

metas.name: Canada - 2 side 1 top
metas.note:
These distinctive pole tops are most commonly found in Ontario. They have two insulators to the side, and one on top. The side insulators are affixed to the pole with a distinct attachment. Sometimes, multiple of them can be stacked on top of each other.

NOTE: They can occasionally appear in British Columbia, Nova Scotia, or other provinces more rarely.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Canada - Quebec pole
metas.note: Some Québec poles have recognizable pole tops with insulator rods that are angled slightly upwards.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Canada - Québec polelabel
metas.note: Québec poles may sometimes have a vertical black and yellow label. There is a small ‘Q’ in the black part.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Canada - Saska pole
metas.note: Pole top insulators in Saskatchewan alternate. While one pole will have one insulator on the left and two on the right, the next will have two on the left and one on the right.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Canada - small white sticker
metas.note: Poles on Prince Edward Island usually feature a small white sticker.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Canada - Transfo 45° angle
metas.note: Transformers on Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia will be installed at a 45° angle relative to the road. On PEI, red numbers will usually be written on the side.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Canada - Transfo faced road
metas.note: The transformers on poles will face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick, while in other provinces, it will be parallel with the wires.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/canada.

metas.name: Chile - pole
metas.note:
Chile uses square concrete poles with an indent on both sides. They are somewhat similar to Brazilian poles, however have fewer horizontal supports in the indent. The upper part typically has small pinholes.

Wooden poles are also fairly common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/chile.

metas.name: Colombia - Antioquia paint
metas.note: These pole markings with one short black strip on the top and bottom, and a longer yellow section in the middle, are most commonly found in the Antioquia department. Sometimes, you can find them in the Cordoba department as well.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/colombia.

metas.name: Colombia - Bogota and Cundinamarca
metas.note: In the departments of Bogotá and Cundinamarca, you will find these pole markings with white paint and orange vertical numbers.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Colombia - Cali
metas.note: In the city of Cali and nearby towns you'll find white vertical numbers on a black background.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Colombia - Cauca
metas.note: These pole markings are unique to the department of Cauca they are characterised by a only blue numbers printed onto a yellow background.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Colombia - Cundinamarca
metas.note: This Blue Horizontal Plate starting with “AP” with a few numbers can only be found in Cundinamarca.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/colombia.

metas.name: Colombia - Huila
metas.note: Hulia has a orange background with black numbers and start with a letter.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Colombia - Narino
metas.note: These pole markings are unique to the department of Nariño. They are characterized by a mix of blue numbers and the letters 'TA' or 'SA' on a yellow background. In the neighboring department, you will also find blue numbers on a yellow background; however, these do not include any letters.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Colombia - orange QR code
metas.note: In the cities of Barranquilla and Santa Marta, you will find orange plastic stickers with a QR code on them.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Colombia - polepaint
metas.note: Colombian poles are often marked with unique black-and-yellow or black-and-orange stripes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/colombia.

metas.name: Colombia - Risaralda and Caldas
metas.note: In Risaralda and Caldas, the pole markings have an orange background with blue numbers that start with a letter. Be careful in Huila the markings can look very similar, but the numbers are black.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Colombia - Santa Marta paint
metas.note: In Santa Marta you can find these light and dark blue pole paints.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/colombia.

metas.name: Colombia - Tolima
metas.note: These pole markings are unique to the department of Tolima. They are characterized by white vertical numbers printed on an orange plastic sticker.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Colombia - Valle del Cauca
metas.note: These pole markings are unique to the department of Valle Del Cauca they are characterised by yellow numbers printed onto a blue background.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/colombia for more clues.

metas.name: Ecuador - holey pole
metas.note: In the south of Ecuador you will find sometimes holey poles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ecuador.

metas.name: Ecuador - waffle pole
metas.note:
The ladder pole. It has a lot of small indents – resembling the steps of a ladder. Within Latin America, these poles are more or less unique to Ecuador.

NOTE: Brazilian waffle poles also have indents, but only a couple – as opposed to the large amount of indents that Ecuadorian ladder poles have.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ecuador.

metas.name: Estonia - metal cap on top
metas.note:
Most wooden poles have a small metal cap on top, similar to those found in the Nordic countries.

NOTE: Alongside the Nordic countries of Sweden, Finland and Norway, these caps can also sometimes be found in Latvia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: Estonia - trident
metas.note: Trident pole tops are somewhat common: This pole top features one insulator on top, and two to the side.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/estonia.

metas.name: France - blue sticker
metas.note:
Small blue rectangular markings on utility poles are unique to France. They are often referred to as ‘stickers’ by the community, but are actually small plates.

You will find these plates on almost all wooden and metallic poles, but not as often on ladder poles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Diamond shaped top
metas.note:
Diamond shaped pole tops with three wires are commonly called “French poletops” within the community. They are most frequently found on top of ladder poles.

NOTE: Within Europe, “French poletops” in conjunction with ladder poles are also common in Spain.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - insulators on top
metas.note: Some variations of the French pole tops have the insulators on top. These variations may resemble an arrowhead and are unique to France.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - ladder poles
metas.note:
Concrete poles with step-like indents are common in France. They are referred to as ladder or waffle poles by the community.

NOTE: They are also common in Spain.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - octagonal metal poles
metas.note: Thin octagonal metal poles are very common in rural areas and small towns.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - spike top
metas.note: It is sometimes hard to distinguish France, Ireland, and the UK. An easy trick is to focus on the tops of the wooden poles: France has a spiked top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Germany - curved top
metas.note: Pole tops which have a curved horizontal bar can be found in Bavaria, though they are rare.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - round concrete pole
metas.note: These round concrete poles with metal brackets are more common in the east of Germany than in the west.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/germany for more clues.

metas.name: Germany - thicker middle part
metas.note: These pole tops where the middle of the horizontal bar is thicker can be found in all of former East Germany.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/germany.

metas.name: Germany - triangle
metas.note:
Triangle pole tops similar to the ones in Czechoslovakia are common in Western Germany.

NOTE: There may be some exceptions outside the highlighted areas.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/germany for more clues.

metas.name: Ghana - pole
metas.note: Ghana typically uses wooden poles with 3 insulators on a metallic crossbar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ghana.

metas.name: Greece - five vertical insulators
metas.note: Many poles in Greece will have five vertical insulators. They can either be attached to the pole or the metal frames from the previous tip.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - harp pole
metas.note: These distinctive poletops, which have a metal frame shaped vaguely like a harp, are unique to Greece.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - lamp with a round shade
metas.note:
This type of small lamp, attached to the side of poles with a round shade above the light bulb.

NOTE: You can also find them in North Macedonia and Serbia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Greece - wooden pole top
metas.note: In Greece you will finde a lot of these wooden crossbar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/greece.

metas.name: Guatemala - completely green pole
metas.note:
Completely green utility poles are primarily found in the southeast of the country, but also on a road in the further north in the east and on a small stretch of road around Melchor de Mencos, near the end of the coverage in the far northeast.

These poles also feature small pole plates, which can further narrow down the road. This will be further explained in the next tip.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/guatemala.

metas.name: Guatemala - painted pole
metas.note: In Guatemala you will very commonly see poles painted with either pink, green or a combination of the two.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/guatemala.

metas.name: Hungary - holey pole
metas.note: Concrete holey poles with medium-sized holes going all the way to the bottom are common. They are similar to those in Poland and Romania, but Polish poles have holes that don't go all the way to the top or bottom, and Romanian poles are usually wider and painted white at the bottom.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/hungary.

metas.name: India - ‘<’ shape top
metas.note: Poles with two diagonal bars forming a ‘<’ shape are common in Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh and occasionally found in Assam.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - black pole sticker
metas.note: On the Andaman and Nicobar Islands you can find these black pole stickers, containing several digits as well as an arrow in the middle.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - concret two sections
metas.note: Poles divided in two sections, in a similar fashion to Brazilian poles, are common in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - concrete holey poles
metas.note:
Concrete holey poles are unique to Gujarat and the Union territory of Daman and Diu, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.

Gujarat uses a variety of poletops, some of which can be used to identify other states. Beware that holey poles generally take precedence over poletop metas.

NOTE: They are rarely found in other states especially Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and Chhattisg
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - concrete trident poletops
metas.note: In Karnataka, and sometimes in Haryana, you can find trident poletops on concrete poles where the central insulator is attached directly to the top of the pole, while the other two are attached to a horizontal crossbar positioned slightly further down. There is also a variant having several bars instead of one.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - mesh pattern
metas.note: Metal poles with a mesh pattern are commonly found in Sikkim.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - metal holey poles
metas.note: Metal holey poles are common in Kerala.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - metal trident pole
metas.note: In Manipur you can often find trident poletops on poles made entirely out of metal. They sometimes have small bars on the top of the trident.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - mint green electricity counters
metas.note: Electricity counters in Punjab are usually mint green with small window-like squares. They can rarely be seen in Haryana.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - short and long crossbar
metas.note: Poletops with a short crossbar above a longer crossbar can be found in Goa.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - tall and narrow rectangle
metas.note: A variety of poletops attached to the pole with two vertical bars forming a tall and narrow rectangle can be found in West Bengal.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - thin grey metal poles
metas.note: Thin grey metal poles are seen all over northeastern India and in the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. You will commonly see two of these poles in close proximity.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - top bend 90°
metas.note: Trident poletops with the tip of the middle bar bent at a 90° angle can be found in Assam.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - two crossbars
metas.note:
In Assam, Meghalaya and Mizoram you commonly see poles with two crossbars, each with two insulators. If there are more than two bars, you should be in Meghalaya or Mizoram.

NOTE: They can rarely be seen in other states.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/india.

metas.name: India - upside down A
metas.note: Poles in Madhya Pradesh often have a metal bar shaped like an upside down A slightly below the top of the pole.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - upside down trapezoid
metas.note:
A connector on the pole which looks like an upside down trapezoid is most common in Chhattisgarh and somewhat common in Meghalaya, Tripura and Maharashtra, but can rarely be found in many other states.

NOTE: They can also be paired with Holey Poles in Gujarat and Ladder Poles in Andhra Pradesh, thus only use the trapezoid when no other pole meta is present-
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - upside down triangle poletops
metas.note: Upside down triangle poletops placed below the top of the pole are commonly found in Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, and less commonly in Madhya Pradesh.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - upside down triangle with crossbars
metas.note: In West Bengal you may also find poletops containing two crossbars which are connected to each other with thin vertical supports on either side. The lower bar is connected on either side to the pole with diagonal supports.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - white black white paint
metas.note: Markings on poles and trees, consisting of one black stripe in-between two white ones, are common in Tamil Nadu.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - window poletop
metas.note: Small metal poletops in the shape of a window are found in Punjab and Haryana.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - yellow black paint
metas.note: Pole paint consisting of exactly four thicker black and yellow stripes can be found in Bihar.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: India - yellow pole markings
metas.note:
Small yellow pole markings are commonly found in Kerala.

NOTE: Similar stickers can rarely be found in other states.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/india for more clues.

metas.name: Indonesia - bali square
metas.note: Bali features both even and uneven poles, as well as the Lesser Sunda island variants. You can also find this unique rectangle attachment on the pole tops in Bali.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - blue and green markings
metas.note: You can often see thin, black poles next to regular poles near the East Peninsula of Central Sulawesi. Two pieces of tape can be seen near the top of the poles, usually light blue and green. These can rarely be seen in northern South East Sulawesi.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - even but uneven
metas.note: These poles are almost exclusive to North Sumatra. The bar which holds the insulators is even, but features uneven insulators with one on one side and two on the other.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - nusas extra support
metas.note: On the Lesser Sunda Islands (“Nusas”), you can find poles with an extra support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - sulawesi extra attachment
metas.note: Pole tops in North and Central Sulawesi, and Gorontalo commonly feature an extra attachment right under the horizontal bar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - triangle attachment
metas.note:
You can find these poles with a triangle attachment under the horizontal bar in the following regions.

NOTE: This does not apply to stacked poles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Indonesia - trident
metas.note: Trident style pole tops are most commonly found in Central Java and Yogyakarta, and rarely in South and West Kalimantan, and North Sumatra and Riau.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/indonesia.

metas.name: Ireland - slanted top
metas.note: It is sometimes hard to distinguish France, Ireland, and the UK. An easy trick is to focus on the tops of the wooden poles: Ireland has a slanted top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Italy - trident
metas.note:
The most common pole tops in Italy are tridents pole tops with a concrete or metall crossbar.

There are several possible configurations of insulators.The two shown in the image are the most common ones.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - white pole sticker
metas.note: Wooden poles in Italy will commonly feature a small white pole sticker.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Akmola Region
metas.note: Akmola region has a very thin layer of red, then white, and a thin layer of black on the bottom.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Atyrau Region
metas.note: Atyrau Region uses blue, white, and black paint.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Ekibastuz
metas.note: Ekibastuz has a thin layer of blue, and white
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Kentau
metas.note: Kentau poles have thin layers of blue, yellow, and red, then blue and black below them.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Kokshetau
metas.note: Kokshetau uses a few designs, but they all have light blue on the bottom, and sometimes, a thin strip, or two, of yellow on top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Kostanay
metas.note: Kostanay uses a thin layer of turqoise, and yellow.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Kyzylorda lamp posts
metas.note: Kyzylorda lamp posts are white, and have turquoise on the bottom.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Kyzylorda poles
metas.note: Kyzylorda poles have a thin layer of yellow and red, then white.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Petropavl
metas.note: Petropavl has a thin layer of white, and light grey.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Rudny
metas.note: Rudny has red, yellow, red on the top, with white below it.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Shchuchinsk
metas.note: Shchuchinsk has a thin layer of red, and yellow.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan for more clues.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Shymkent
metas.note: Shymkent poles have a thin layer of yellow and red, then green.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - Taraz
metas.note: Taraz has red, yellow, and black.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kazakhstan - West Kazakhstan
metas.note: West Kazakhstan Region uses red, white, and black paint.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kazakhstan.

metas.name: Kenya - Pole
metas.note:
Kenya use wooden poles with a metallic topbar and support.

NOTE: Panama use mostly concrete poles with wooden support. Good to know for 50/50
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/kenya for more clues.

metas.name: Kyrgyzstan - pole paint
metas.note:
These towns east and west of Bishkek feature these colourful poles with yellow, green, white, and sometimes red on top.

NOTE: Sokuluk will not have the red paint on top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/kyrgyzstan.

metas.name: Latvia - hook-shaped insulators
metas.note:
Latvian poles have distinctive poletops, with hook-shaped insulators, that are arranged in an alternating manner: left-right-left (or vice versa).

NOTE: These poletops are much more rare in the other two Baltic countries. They can however appear in some other European countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/latvia.

metas.name: Lithuania - concrete support beam
metas.note:
Lithuanian poles are usually square and concrete, and often feature a diagonal support beam.

NOTE: While most common in Lithuania, these are also found from time to time in Estonia, and on rare occasions in Latvia. In Estonia and Latvia wooden poles with a support beam are much more common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Lithuania - pole tops
metas.note:
Pictured here are some typical Lithuanian poletops.

They often have short horizontal rods, on which the insulators are placed.

In some poletops, the insulators are arranged in a trident-like shape, with one on top, and two on each side.

Note that these poletops are not unique to Lithuania: they can also be found in the other post-Soviet countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/lithuania.

metas.name: Malaysia - black sticker
metas.note: Black pole stickers are only found on electricity poles in mainland Malaysia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malaysia.

metas.name: Malaysia - Black sticker ‘TEL TNB’
metas.note: Black stickers with the text ‘TEL TNB’ at the bottom, are only found in Johor.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malaysia.

metas.name: Malaysia - lamp boomerang
metas.note:
This lamp post with a supporting piece of sheet metal resembling a boomerang is found in Sarawak.

NOTE: It is more common in cities other than Kuching.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malaysia.

metas.name: Malaysia - lamp triangular metal support
metas.note: Lamp posts with a triangular metal support are mainly found on mainland Malaysia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malaysia.

metas.name: Malaysia - lamp two small circles
metas.note: Lamp posts with two small circles on the support are mainly found on mainland Malaysia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malaysia.

metas.name: Malaysia - Sabah pole
metas.note: Thin metal poles with two parallel pole tops are exclusive to the Sabah region of Borneo.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malaysia.

metas.name: Malaysia - Sarawak pole
metas.note:
Electricity poles on the Borneo side typically have a 2-1 insulator configuration, and a long diagonal wooden support. They are exclusive to the Sarawak region of the island.

NOTE: Indonesian poles can look similar, but they are usually not made of wood, and use smaller or no diagonal supports.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malaysia.

metas.name: Malaysia - white sticker
metas.note: White pole stickers are only found on electricity poles on the island of Borneo, in Sarawak.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malaysia.

metas.name: Mexico - asymmetric crossbar and double-stacked
metas.note: Poles with an asymmetric crossbar and double-stacked insulators are exclusive to Mexico City, State of Mexico, Hidalgo, and Morelos.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - mesh body
metas.note: Poles with a mesh body are most commonly found in San Luis Potosi, Guanajuato, and Queretaro.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - single support
metas.note: Poles with a lowered crossbar and a single support beam that extend from one end of the crossbar to the pole itself can be found in Durango.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - suspended below
metas.note: These concrete poles with insulators suspended below the crossbars are unique to the Yucatan peninsula.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - white insulator
metas.note: White insulators that are shaped like acorns can be found along the coastal states of Mexico, but are by far most common in Michoacan, Colima, and Veracruz.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - wooden lowered crossbar
metas.note: Wooden poles with a lowered crossbar are mostly found in Sinaloa and Sonora.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Mexico - wooden suspended below
metas.note: The wooden variant of the hanging pole is found on the Baja California peninsula.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/mexico.

metas.name: Namibia - A-Frame
metas.note: Poles with 3 bars forming the letter ‘A’, with the bottom insulators being attached at the edges of a horizontal bar, can be found everywhere in Namibia. It is a good clue for Namibia in a Kenya or Oman 50/50.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/namibia for more clues.

metas.name: Namibia - alternating insulators
metas.note: Poles with 3 alternating insulators sticking out horizontally at the top. This pole can be found everywhere in Namibia. It is a good clue for Namibia in a Kenya or Oman 50/50.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/namibia for more clues.

metas.name: Namibia - birdpole
metas.note: It features mostly 1 horizontal bars with thin white insulators that resemble rows of birds, which is why they are referred to as “bird poles” in the community. It is a good clue for Namibia in a Kenya or Oman 50/50.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/namibia for more clues.

metas.name: New Zealand - black sticker 5 digits
metas.note: A medium sized black vertical sticker with 5 digits is found in West Coast, Tasman, southern Canterbury and southern Northland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - black sticker 6 digits
metas.note:
A long black vertical sticker with 6 digits with a small black square beneath it, is found on most of the North Island, in Southland and in Otago. On the North Island the first digit will be a 3 or a 4, while on the South Island it starts with an 8.

NOTE: There is a similar regional black sticker with 6 digits but without a small square below it. Additionally, the sticker can rarely be white.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - holey pole
metas.note: Holey poles are found most commonly in Southland and around Auckland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - horizontal black sticker
metas.note: A small black horizontal pole sticker, with several numbers, is often found in Taranaki and Wellington. The sticker may rarely be found in parts of Manawatū-Whanganui, Waikato, and southern Hawke's Bay.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - horizontal white sticker
metas.note:
Similarly, a small white horizontal pole sticker with several numbers is found in several parts of the North Island.

NOTE: The edges of the plate must be straight, meaning they cannot be rounded. Rounded plates are seen all across the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - long silver possum guard
metas.note: Many of the utility poles in Southland feature a long cylindrical silver possum guard. These are also more rarely found in western Otago.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - olive brown possum guard
metas.note: Most utility poles in the Marlborough region have a long square shaped olive-brown possum guard. These can appear alongside the usual shorter silver possum guards.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - orange paint
metas.note: Poles near Timaru often have a tall rectangle of orange paint on them with the text “DANGER LIVE WIRES”.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - square concrete pole
metas.note: Square concrete poles without the usual indent are most common in Southland, but can also be found in Otago, Taranaki and Manawatū-Whanganui.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - tall metal bar
metas.note:
Poles with the middle insulator being installed on top of a tall metal bar are often found along the Auckland Waikato border, as well as in other parts of Waikato.

NOTE: Insulators installed on significantly shorter vertical bars are rarer and can be found all across the country.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - uneven crossbar
metas.note: Uneven crossbars, meaning they are off-centre, are found in Otago, Marlborough, Wellington and Taranaki.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - white paint
metas.note: Some concrete poles in eastern Waikato and Whanganui city have white paint on the middle part of their wooden crossbars. This white painted crossbar can also be found in parts of western Bay of Plenty, Taranaki, Manawatū-Whanganui and eastern Wellington.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - yellow tag
metas.note: A yellow tag, similar in appearance to a cow-tag, is found on most poles in Gisborne. It is also found in a few spots on the South Island, as well as over the border in northern Hawke’s Bay.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: New Zealand - yellow warning sticker
metas.note: A warning sticker attached to poles, which has a yellow danger triangle between two white rectangles, is found in Hawke’s Bay, from lake Taupo to lake Rotorua, in northern Waikato and south of Auckland city.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/new-zealand.

metas.name: Nigeria - pole
metas.note: Most Nigerian poles are made of concrete, have indents with a few horizontal supports, and are similar to the ones used in Brazil, but do not have holes through them.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/nigeria.

metas.name: Panama - horizontal marker
metas.note: East of Panama City and around Colon, utility pole marker are white or yellow and vertical.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/panama for more clues.

metas.name: Panama - round concrete
metas.note:
Panama uses a wide variety of poles, but the most common type is a round concrete pole.

NOTE: Kenya has most of the time wooden poles with metallic support while Panama typically use wooden support.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/panama.

metas.name: Panama - thin vertical marker
metas.note: Thin yellow plates, vertical or horizontal, with a visible black border are most common in the Colón Province.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/panama for more clues.

metas.name: Panama - vertical marker
metas.note:
The eastern provinces often have tall vertical plates that can be yellow or white. They are commonly attached to poles by black zip ties.

NOTE: Be careful there are white vertical plates, often attached by metallic zip ties. They are slightly wider than the eastern plates and always have 6 digits.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/panama for more clues.

metas.name: Philippines - chilie style pole
metas.note: Square concrete poles with an indent on both side, similar to the poles found in Chile, are mainly found north of Manila and in and around the city of Bacolod on the island of Negros.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/philippines.

metas.name: Philippines - L-shaped cross section
metas.note:
A poletop made up of two tall vertical metal bars having an L-shaped cross-section which are connected via several thin wires, making it resemble a ladder, is unique to Manila and the surrounding area.

NOTE: You may sometimes come across similar looking poletops, with square bars instead of L-shaped ones, throughout the entire country. They will however almost never have more than two connecting wires.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/philippines.

metas.name: Philippines - Octagonal metal poles
metas.note:
Octagonal metal poles are quite common in the Philippines.

NOTE: They can sometimes be found in Bangladesh and some parts of Malaysia as well.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/philippines.

metas.name: Philippines - Square metal mesh poles
metas.note:
Square metal mesh poles are found on Mindanao, mainly on the Zamboanga peninsula.

NOTE: Most of the poles found outside of the Zamboanga peninsula are found along highways and have poletops with three hanging insulators.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/philippines.

metas.name: Poland - holey pole
metas.note: Holey poles with smaller holes are common in Poland. Similar poles can be found in Hungary and Romania, but in Poland, the holes don't extend all the way to the bottom or the top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/poland.

metas.name: Portugal - ladder pole with holes
metas.note:
Concrete ladder poles, with very tall ladder steps, are common in Portugal. Each step often has a small see-through hole.

NOTE: In Spain and France you will commonly see ladder poles with short steps.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Romania - green tag
metas.note: A small green Tag with 2 letters and a few digits. The two letters are the abbreviations of the county.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - holey pole
metas.note: Concrete holey poles with wide holes and usually painted white at the bottom are common in Romania. They are similar to poles in Poland and Hungary, but Polish poles have smaller holes that don’t go all the way to the bottom or top, and Hungarian poles typically have smaller holes as well.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - large yellow sticker
metas.note:
Large yellow sticker with the town name on it.

NOTE: Yellow sticker are common everywhere in Romania, but there are significant smaller.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - triangle top
metas.note:
These pole tops, with an upside down triangle shape, are a good clue for Romania.

NOTE: Serbia, Czechia, Slovakia and Alabania use similar pole tops.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Romania - white sticker
metas.note:
A white sticker with a round waring symbole is common in the north-west of Romania.

NOTE: White stickers can be found everywhere in Romania, but they usually have a triangular warning symbol.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/romania.

metas.name: Russia - pole shields
metas.note: Black & white-striped pole shields are common along highways, especially in European Russia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/russia.

metas.name: Senegal - pole
metas.note: Being a former French colony, Senegal uses French infrastructure like poles.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/senegal for more clues.

metas.name: Serbia - metal mesh
metas.note: Metal poles, either in the shape of a ladder or with a mesh pattern, are common in small town. If you find a random metal pole inside a town, it is probably Serbia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/serbia.

metas.name: Slovakia - concrete support
metas.note:
It is somewhat more common to see wooden poles, and in turn, white concrete supports in Slovakia rather than in Czechia.

Note that because there are many variables, it may sometimes be inconsistent. Therefore, this information should preferably be used to help decide between a difficult fifty-fifty.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovakia.

metas.name: Slovakia/Czechia - double round concrete
metas.note: Czechia and Slovakia most commonly use wide, round concrete poles, which are quite often attached in pairs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Slovakia/Czechia - short metal bars
metas.note: Czech and Slovak pole tops typically feature short metal bars that hold the insulators.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Slovakia/Czechia - triangle top
metas.note:
Two support bars holding up the metal bar on pole tops, resembling an upside down triangle, can sometimes be found in Czechia and Slovakia.

NOTE: This is also found in Germany, Albania, Serbia and Romania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Slovakia/Czechia - trident
metas.note: You may also see concrete poles with trident poletops, with two arms angled upwards. The number of insulators and other details will vary, however the general shape will be the same. Out of the pole tops listed, these are the least common, but unique to the two countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: South Africa - 1 or 2 metal arms
metas.note: Poles with 1 or 2 metal arms holding up insulators are most commonly seen in Mpumalanga.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/south-africa.

metas.name: South Africa - 2 diagonal bars
metas.note: Poles with 2 diagonal bars forming a ‘<’ shape can be found mostly in the northeastern provinces, most commonly in Limpopo and North West.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/south-africa.

metas.name: South Africa - 3 alternating insulators
metas.note: Poles with 3 alternating insulators sticking out horizontally at the top are mostly seen in the four northern provinces of Limpopo, Gauteng, North West and Mpumalanga. They can also sometimes be found in Northern Cape. In the rest of the country, these pole tops are exceedingly rare.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/south-africa.

metas.name: South Africa - A poletop
metas.note: Poles with 3 bars forming the letter ‘A’, with the bottom insulators being attached at the edges of a horizontal bar, can be found almost exclusively in Western Cape, and rarely in bordering provinces.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/south-africa for more clues.

metas.name: South Africa - bird pole
metas.note: The most common type of pole in South Africa features 1 to 5 horizontal bars with thin white insulators that resemble rows of birds, which is why they are referred to as “bird poles” in the community.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/south-africa for more clues.

metas.name: South Africa - Trident Pole
metas.note: Trident pole tops are almost unique to KwaZulu-Natal.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/south-africa for more clues.

metas.name: South Africa - wide A poletop
metas.note: A similar poletop can be found in Eastern Cape, however the A-shape is noticeably wider and the bottom insulators are attached directly to the ‘A’ rather than a horizontal bar.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/south-africa.

metas.name: South Korea - black and yellow diagonal stripes
metas.note:
Utility poles almost always have these pole markings near the bottom, consisting of black and yellow diagonal stripes.

These markings look similar to the ones found in Taiwan. There are however two main differences:

In South Korea, the stripes do not reach all the way to the bottom, whereas in Taiwan they do.

In South Korea, the stripes are more yellow. In Taiwan, they have more of an orange tint.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/south-korea.

metas.name: South Korea - spike
metas.note: Most poles in South Korea have a tapered “spike” on top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/south-korea.

metas.name: Spain - french style
metas.note:
“French style” poletops are common in Spain. They are shaped like an upside down triangle, with a horizontal top bar that is curved slightly upwards. They are usually found on top of tall ladder poles or medium sized steel poles.

NOTE: As the name suggests, French poletops are also very common in France.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - ladder pole
metas.note:
In Spain, you can find a variety of electricity poles and pole tops. In small towns and sparsely populated rural areas concrete ladder poles and wooden poles are the most common.

“Ladder” poles have indents that resemble a ladder, hence the name.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - pylons
metas.note: High voltage electricity lines supported by pylons are very common in Spain, especially compared to other Mediterranean countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - steel mesh rectangular
metas.note: Poles with a steel mesh structure making rectangular shapes instead of the typical triangles can be found in the southern half of Spain, and are particularly common in Murcia and southern Alicante.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Sri Lanka - concrete holey pole
metas.note: Poles with large see-through holes in the lower half of the pole (“holey poles“). These poles are unique to Sri Lanka.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sri-lanka.

metas.name: Sri Lanka - concrete square pole
metas.note:
Square poles with small pinholes in the sides. These pinholes are limited to the top part of the pole.

NOTE: The square poles with small pinholes can look very similar to those found in Thailand. However, in Thailand the pinholes extend all the way to the bottom of the pole.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/sri-lanka.

metas.name: Taiwan - pole markings
metas.note:
Poles almost always feature these black and yellow diagonal-striped markings that run all the way to the bottom.

NOTE: Similar markings can be seen in South Korea. However, the markings are much shorter and do not run all the way to the bottom.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/taiwan.

metas.name: Taiwan - pole top
metas.note: Like Cambodia Taiwan has round concrete poles with small holes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/taiwan.

metas.name: Thailand - 2 insulators
metas.note: Conversely, poles with two insulators on the crossbar can be found in the rest of the country.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/thailand for more clues.

metas.name: Thailand - chilestyle pole
metas.note:
Regular poles with a Chilean style indent are found around Bangkok.

NOTE: Larger and thicker poles with indents are found on highways all throughout the country.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/thailand for more clues.

metas.name: Thailand - Insulators 7 or more ridges
metas.note:
Insulators with 7 or more ridges are found in the southern half of the peninsula, as well as highways in Chiang Rai and Phayao.

NOTE: In the north, you may still find 5 or 6 ridges on insulators, as these are the standard amount throughout the country.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/thailand for more clues.

metas.name: Thailand - one insulator
metas.note: Poles with only one insulator on the crossbar can be found from south on the peninsula from Ranong and Chumphon.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/thailand for more clues.

metas.name: Turkey - metal pole
metas.note: Metal poles, either in the shape of a ladder or with a mesh pattern, are extremely common in Turkey.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/turkey for more clues.

metas.name: United kingdom - flat pole top
metas.note: It is sometimes hard to distinguish France, Ireland, and the UK. An easy trick is to focus on the tops of the wooden poles: UK has a flat top
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United kingdom - pole steps
metas.note:
The UK uses wooden poles. Pole steps bolted on the side of the pole are very common. These pole steps are shaped like a series of thin horizontal metal rods.

NOTE: Ireland also commonly uses wooden poles with pole steps.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United States - California 3 yellow stripes
metas.note: Utility poles in California usually have markings at the bottom of the pole that consist of 3 yellow stripes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - horizontal yellow plate
metas.note:
In Utah, Wyoming and southeast Idaho these yellow plates are pretty common.

NOTE: can be found rarely also in Whashington, Oregon and California
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/united-states for more clues.

metas.name: United States - vertical silver/gold plate
metas.note: In Rhode Island and Massachusetts, you’ll often find silver or gold-colored vertical plates near the base of utility poles.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/united-states for more clues.

metas.name: United States - Wisconsin pole sticker
metas.note: A rectangular white metal plate, with an orange rectangle and diamond, can be seen on most poles in Wisconsin and the Michigan peninsula.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-states.

metas.name: United States - yellow net
metas.note: In southeastern Pennsylvania, utility poles often have yellow mesh/net near the base.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/united-states for more clues.

metas.name: United States - yellow single sticker
metas.note: In newer coverage of Hawaii, you will often see horizontal yellow sticker on poles.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/united-states for more clues.

metas.name: Uruguay - flat metal sheets
metas.note:
Round poles with a pole top consisting of flat metal sheets.

In addition, you might see simple wooden poles with one insulator, as well as very rarely some Argentina-style poles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/uruguay.

metas.name: Uruguay - square concrete
metas.note:
Square concrete poles is in South America a good clue for Uruguay.

In addition, you might see simple wooden poles with one insulator, as well as very rarely some Argentina-style poles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/uruguay.

metas.name: Uruguay - trident
metas.note:
Uruguay uses a handful of different utility poles. One very common and useful one are the so-called trident poles, which get their name from their distinctive pole tops with three insulators that point upwards.

NOTE: Similar trident poles can be found in the neighbouring Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/uruguay.

metas.name: Vietnam - (half) trapezoid support
metas.note: Trapezoid support is where you have a crossbar with a diagonal support attached to a small horizontal segment below. This forms a trapezoid underneath the bar. As you can see in the images, it can be seen on both sides or just one half of it.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - black pole sticker
metas.note: Black pole stickers are common in the north of Vietnam
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - central A-top
metas.note: Central A top is where you can see an A standing on the crossbar. It can be centered or off to the side. It is almost exclusively found in central Vietnam.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - cone guard
metas.note: A cone shaped possum guard.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - extended/raised pole
metas.note: Extended top is where the top of the pole is extended with something like a metal frame. It is mainly found south, but can rarely be seen everywhere.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - half holey
metas.note: Holey poles are concrete squared poles with holes going through the pole at the bottom. Holey poles in general are found more commonly north, but there are three distinct variations of this. The half holey pole is found throughout the entire country.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - holey 3/4
metas.note: This holey pole has holes until about 3/4 upwards and is unique to the north. The standard holey pole can be found everywhere.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - mini bars
metas.note:
Mini bars are super short L shaped crossbars on top of poles. They usually have small spools on top. They are generally found north, but reach quite far south as well.

NOTE: In the north they are usually mounted on holey poles whereas in the central region they are usually mounted on pinhole poles
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - mounted spools
metas.note: Mounted spools are spools mounted directly to the pole. In opposition to the mini bars where spools can also be found. It is almost exclusive to the far south of the country.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - offset-mounted lamp
metas.note:
This lamp sometimes connected to utility poles is the Offset mounted lamp. It is attached to the pole with two metal bars and is quite far out from the pole. It is found in the south of the country.

NOTE: There are similar looking lamps.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - one sided top
metas.note: One sided top is where the pole has the crossbar on one side with a single diagonal support beam. It can either be completely on one side or uneven to one side. Important to note that you should not confuse it with trapezoid support which has an extra horizontal segment in the support beam. It is almost exclusively found in the far south.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - pin hole pole
metas.note: Pinhole poles are round concrete poles with small pin holes at the top. It is by far the most common pole in Vietnam. The poletop does not matter and it can also be found doubled up. It is super common south, but can rarely be seen north as well.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - plain round concrete
metas.note: The plain concrete pole has no holes in it. The pole top does not matter and it can also be found doubled up, with two next to each other. Most common in the north.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - silver band
metas.note: A silver band — it is probably a possum guard. You will find them in the south and rarely in the central regions.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - south triangle
metas.note: South triangle is where you can see small metal bars in a triangle shape underneath the crossbar. Important to note is the lack of a horizontal segment in between the two diagonal segments (that would make it a trapezoid). The two supports should touch in the middle.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - triple half trapezium pole support
metas.note: This pole top is just the trapezoid support but stacked on top of each other three times. It overlaps with the trapezoid region, but is exclusive to the far north.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - twin holey pole
metas.note: Two holey poles back to back. Can be with half holey poles and with 3/4 holey poles. Twin holey poles are common in the north.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.

metas.name: Vietnam - twin poles
metas.note: Like in Czechia and Slovakia, concrete poles attached in pairs are very common and is a good clue for Vietnam.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/vietnam.

metas.name: Vietnam - ultra tall pole
metas.note: Ultra tall poles are like the name suggests, Ultra tall. It is almost as if they stacked two poles on top of each other, signified by the small brown section 1/3 up the pole. They are mainly found north, but are also rarely found everywhere else.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/vietnam for more clues.
